newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-HAVELANGE REFUSES TO BE DRAWN INTO 2006 ROW.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HAVELANGE REFUSES TO BE DRAWN INTO 2006 ROW.

text.p: FIFA president Joao Havelange maintained a diplomatic neutrality on Saturday when he refused to be drawn into the bidding war between England and Germany for the right to stage the 2006 World Cup finals.
The two European countries are among a number who have said they want to host the finals in nine years time -- the decision on which will be taken in June 2000.
But Havelange, who, the Germans claim, said three years ago he was supporting their bid, gave nothing away on Saturday.

"On one side, FIFA is happy and proud that nine associations have shown an interest in staging the 2006 World Cup finals, especially when the plans for the 2002 finals are still being put into place," he said.

"One has to say that the first association to show their interest was Germany. Concerning the candidature of England, in Wembley one has a stadium which would be worthy of hosting any World Cup final, " he said.

England and Germany have been engaged in a fierce battle of words and wit over the last month when it emerged that UEFA had given Germany their backing for a bid without due consultation with their members.
Over the last month the battle between the two countries has intensified, although FIFA have said it was perfectly acceptable for two countries from the same continent to bid for the finals.
But what FIFA wants to avoid is a similar situation to the 2002 finals which will be jointly staged by Japan and South Korea.

Havelange, attending a meeting of the law-making International Football Board in Belfast, said Russia, South Africa, Morocco, Egypt, Brazil, Argentina and Australia had also submitted proposals concerning hosting the 2006 finals.

Although the finals are still a considerable number of years away, the battle to influence the decision on where they will be held, was being maintained in Paris on Friday night when Franz Beckenbauer called on UEFA, European soccer's governing body, to support Germany's bid.

"The German Federation asked me to represent them and I hope that UEFA will confirm Germany as the lone European candidate, maybe as soon as their next executive committee meeting on April 17," Beckenbauer told a news conference.

Beckenbauer, the only man to both captain and then manage a World Cup winning team, which he did with West Germany in 1974 and 1990, was in Paris to meet France 1998 World Cup co-chairmen Michel Platini and Fernand Sastre.
"I wanted to know a little more about the way France is financially handling the next World Cup and what we could learn from it," Beckenbauer said.

Beckenbauer, who has been mentioned as a possible successor to Havelange when the 80-year-old Brazilian steps down from the presidency in the summer of 1998, did not dismiss the idea down out of hand on Friday.
"I can't say this opportunity does not interest me. I read laudatory words from Havelange to me in the papers. But I prefer to take one thing at a time," he said.

Havelange himself also referred to the upcoming battle for his position in Belfast. When asked his views on Franco Carraro, the newly-elected chairman of the Italian League succeeding him, Havelange replied: "I have no doubt he would make a very good president if elected."
Lennart Johansson, UEFA's Swedish president is strongly tipped to succeed Havelange, while Issa Hayatou of Cameroon, head of the African Confederation, is another possibility.
